section.title: Hezekiah's Illness and Recovery
section.sectionRationale: Within the Hezekiah narrative interlude, chapters 36 to 39, this chapter turns from public deliverance from Assyria to a private crisis: the king's own mortal illness. Hezekiah's tearful prayer, the LORD's gracious answer of fifteen added years, and his own written song of near death and rescued life prepare the reader for the far larger crisis of exile that the next two chapters begin to unfold.
section.thesis: Facing a death sentence from the LORD's own mouth, Hezekiah weeps and prays rather than simply resigning himself to it, and the LORD who is sovereign even over the sun's shadow graciously adds fifteen years to his life, teaching that prayer reaches the ear of God even when His will has already been announced.
section.frameNote: Six movements: Hezekiah's mortal illness announced; his prayer and bitter weeping; the LORD's answer of fifteen years and a sign in the sun's shadow; Hezekiah's own written song of descent toward Sheol; his song of thanksgiving for restored life; and a closing note on the means of healing and the sign requested.

verses.text: In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’”

units.label: Hezekiah's prayer and tears
units.note: remember how I have walked before You

verses.text: Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD,
saying, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what was good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.

units.label: The LORD's answer: fifteen years and a sign
units.note: the shadow goes back ten steps

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to Isaiah, saying,
“Go and tell Hezekiah that this is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.
And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city.
This will be a sign to you from the LORD that He will do what He has promised:
I will make the sun's shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.’” So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.

units.label: Hezekiah's song: descent toward Sheol
units.note: I must go through the gates of the dead

verses.text: This is a writing by Hezekiah king of Judah after his illness and recovery:
I said, “In the prime of my life I must go through the gates of {{sheol|Sheol}} and be deprived of the remainder of my years.”
I said, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living; I will no longer look on mankind with those who dwell in this world.
My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent. I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom; from day until night You make an end of me.
I composed myself until the morning. Like a lion He breaks all my bones; from day until night You make an end of me.
I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove. My eyes grow weak as I look upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.”

units.label: Hezekiah's song: thanksgiving for restored life
units.note: You have cast all my sins behind Your back

verses.text: What can I say? He has spoken to me, and He Himself has done this. I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul.
O Lord, by such things men live, and in all of them my spirit finds life. You have restored me to health and have let me live.
Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back.
For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You. Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness.
The {{chai|living}}, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.
The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD.
Now Isaiah had said, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.”
And Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?”

sheol.gloss: The realm of the dead, the shadowy world beneath, not yet the fuller revelation of heaven and hell later Scripture unfolds. Hezekiah dreads its gates because there, he says, the dead cannot praise God among the living, which is exactly why his rescue from its brink becomes an occasion for public thanksgiving rather than private relief alone.

chai.gloss: Living, alive, from the root chayah, to live. Hezekiah insists that only the living can thank God and tell the next generation of His faithfulness, so his added years are not merely personal gain but a fresh opportunity to testify, a theme that runs through Scripture's whole understanding of why God grants life and health.

basic.context: Hezekiah receives the hardest possible word from Isaiah: he is dying, and he will not recover. Rather than accepting this in silence, he turns to the wall and weeps bitterly in prayer, reminding God of his faithful life. The LORD hears him, adds fifteen years, confirms it with an extraordinary sign in the sun's shadow, and Hezekiah later writes his own poem describing both his terror at death's approach and his gratitude at being rescued.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical episode, also told in 2 Kings 20 and 2 Chronicles 32, placed here after the Assyrian deliverance to prepare for the Babylonian envoys of chapter 39 and the exile that the Book of Comfort, beginning in chapter 40, will address. It shows that a word from God announcing His will is not necessarily unconditional or unchangeable when met with humble, faithful prayer, without suggesting that every prayer for healing will be answered so visibly.
basic.originalLanguages: Hezekiah dreads passing through the gates of {{sheol}}, the realm of the dead, where he says the dead cannot praise God. His whole argument for wanting to live rests on being among the {{chai}}, the living, who alone can thank the LORD and teach the next generation His faithfulness, a reason for longing to live that reaches beyond mere self-preservation.
basic.typology: Hezekiah's descent in thought to the gates of death and his rescue back to the land of the living, followed immediately by public thanksgiving, anticipates the pattern later fulfilled fully in Christ, who actually entered death and was raised to life never to die again, securing life for His people beyond anything a mere extension of years could offer.
basic.christ: Hezekiah's prayer with bitter weeping over a sentence of death, and God's compassionate answer, echoes forward to Christ, who 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' Hebrews 5:7. Hezekiah's testimony that the LORD 'cast all my sins behind Your back,' verse 17, anticipates the far greater and final casting away of sin accomplished at the cross, where Christ's own death, not a sundial's reversed shadow, is the decisive sign that God keeps His word.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the sun's shadow, able to give a sign that reverses the ordinary course of a day, yet He is also the God who hears the tears of one man and adjusts the very length of his life in response to prayer. He is not moved by cold necessity but genuinely responsive to those who bring their fear and grief honestly before Him.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 20:1-11 and 2 Chronicles 32:24-26 narrate the same illness and healing. Psalm 30 is a similar song of thanksgiving after being rescued from death. Micah 7:19 uses the same image of casting sins away, into the depths of the sea. Hebrews 5:7 describes Christ's own prayers with loud cries and tears in the face of death.
basic.oneStory: Hezekiah's brush with death and his rescued, thankful life is a small window into the whole Bible's pattern: God hears the cries of those who fear death, and grants life not merely for its own sake but so His faithfulness can be told to the next generation. That pattern reaches its full and final form in Christ, who conquered death itself so that His people might live and praise God forever.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a poem in a prose frame. Verses 1 to 8 are narrative, verses 9 to 20 are a 'writing' in Hezekiah's own voice, and verses 21 and 22 are two loose ends tied off at the close. Isaiah's compiler has placed the poem at the centre and let the prose do the setting and the footnotes.

The poem itself turns on a hinge at verse 15. Before it, everything is lament: 'I said' opens verse 10 and again verse 11, and the cry 'from day until night You make an end of me' is repeated word for word in verses 12 and 13, like a man who cannot stop saying the thing that terrifies him. The images keep shrinking a life: a shepherd's tent pulled up and carried off, a weaver's cloth cut from the loom, a lion crushing bones, a bird chirping weakly. After the hinge, 'What can I say?', the vocabulary reverses. The lament had a God who 'makes an end'; the thanksgiving has the same God who 'restores' and 'delivers'. Verses 18 and 19 then set death and life side by side in a tight contrast, and verse 20 closes on the house of the LORD.

That last phrase matters for the ending. Verse 22 asks, 'What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?' So the song ends at the temple and the chapter ends with a question about reaching it. Verses 21 and 22 are also out of order compared with the parallel in 2 Kings 20:7 to 8, and they begin with a flashback ('Now Isaiah had said'). Placing them after the poem keeps the poem as the climax and leaves the poultice as a footnote.

The chapter also answers its neighbour. In Isaiah 37:1 and 37:14 Hezekiah took a public crisis to the house of the LORD. Here, alone and facing a wall, he takes a private crisis to the same God. The promise of verse 6, 'I will defend this city,' repeats the language of Isaiah 37:35 and ties the two chapters into one deliverance.
context.historical:
The dates are tied together by arithmetic inside the Bible. Hezekiah was twenty-five when he became king and reigned twenty-nine years, 2 Kings 18:2. Sennacherib attacked the fortified cities in Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Isaiah 36:1. Fifteen added years from the illness would end a twenty-nine year reign exactly if the sickness fell in that same fourteenth year, which is why the LORD can promise in verse 6 to rescue the king and the city from Assyria in one breath. The Assyrian threat was already on the horizon while the king lay dying.

The illness also threatened the house of David. Manasseh was twelve when he became king, 2 Kings 21:1, which means he was not born until about three years after the recovery. At the time of the sentence, no son who would later reign had yet been born, so the 'God of your father David,' verse 5, was being asked to keep a promise as well as a man. Hezekiah was a reforming king who had opened and repaired the temple doors in his first year, 2 Chronicles 29:1 to 3, which is the background to his claim of wholehearted devotion in verse 3.

The 'stairway of Ahaz' is named for Hezekiah's own father, the king who had refused to ask for any sign, Isaiah 7:12. The text gives no engineering detail of how the steps and the shadow worked, and it is wise not to supply any. Hezekiah, by contrast, asks for a sign in verse 22.

The poultice is a plain piece of ancient medicine: a pressed cake of figs applied to a boil. The word for boil is the one used of the plague on Egypt, Exodus 9:9, and of Job's sores, Job 2:7. Medicine and miracle sit together in the story without competing.

Finally, the sign was noticed abroad. Chronicles says the Babylonian ambassadors came 'to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land,' 2 Chronicles 32:31, which is the bridge into the next chapter.
context.canonical:
The same event is told in 2 Kings 20:1 to 11 and summarised in 2 Chronicles 32:24, but only Isaiah preserves the poem. Isaiah's version also relocates the poultice and the request for a sign to the end, so the Isaiah account is arranged around the song, not around the sequence of events.

Hezekiah's argument for being kept alive is an old one. Psalm 6:5 asks, 'who can praise You from Sheol?'; Psalm 30:9 asks, 'Will the dust praise You?'; Psalm 88:10 to 12 piles up questions about wonders, loving devotion and faithfulness in the grave; and Psalm 115:17 says plainly, 'It is not the dead who praise the LORD.' The songs of lament share one conviction: the worship of God is the point of life.

The poem finds an echo in Jonah's prayer from the fish, where the same word for 'pit' appears and where Jonah says, 'You raised my life from the pit,' Jonah 2:6, and cf. Isaiah 38:17. Jesus then names that prayer's story as the one sign He would give, Matthew 12:39 and 40.

The gloom of verse 18 is not where the Old Testament stays. Psalm 49:15 says, 'God will redeem my life from Sheol,' Isaiah 25:8 says He 'will swallow up death forever,' Isaiah 26:19 says 'Your dead will live,' and Daniel 12:2 speaks of awakening. The New Testament finishes the movement. Peter hears Psalm 16:10 fulfilled when Christ was not abandoned to Hades, Acts 2:24 to 27, and the risen Lord says, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18. Paul can taunt the old enemy with 'Where, O Death, is your victory?' 1 Corinthians 15:55.

Verse 17's 'cast all my sins behind Your back' belongs with Micah 7:19, which pictures sins cast 'into the depths of the sea,' and with Psalm 103:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The compiler of Isaiah wants the reader to ask what a king does with a death sentence, and then to ask what he does with the years that follow. The first question is answered in this chapter: he prays, and the God who sentenced him hears. The second is answered in the next.

The contrast with Ahaz is deliberate. Ahaz was invited to 'ask for a sign from the LORD' and refused with pious words, Isaiah 7:11 and 12. Hezekiah asks, and receives. Isaiah wants the reader to see faith as willingness to ask God for something concrete.

He also wants the reader to hear the poem and notice what it values. The king does not simply celebrate being alive; he says life exists so that 'fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness,' verse 19. A gift of time is a gift of testimony. And the chapter is quietly tied to the city's fate by the promise of verse 6, which says that the king's health and Jerusalem's safety are both held in the same hand.

The first hearers, many of them facing exile, would take heart that the LORD sees tears. But the book is already pointing ahead. Hezekiah receives fifteen more years, and the book will not let us forget what he does with them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is narrative, and the poem is a record of one man's experience. Hezekiah's claim to have 'walked before You faithfully' is reported, not commanded as a formula. It is neither a model for bargaining with God nor a rebuke for appealing to a faithful life; Psalm 18:20 shows a godly person doing something similar. What the chapter commends is bringing the real situation to the LORD with tears and honesty.

The poem's statements about Sheol describe how death looked to a frightened man before the resurrection was revealed. They are not a full doctrine of what happens after death, any more than the bleak verses of Ecclesiastes 9:5 are. The poultice of figs is likewise recorded, not prescribed: Scripture neither forbids medicine nor makes it a requirement, and nothing here says that prayer replaces treatment or the reverse.

The backward-running shadow is a unique sign given to one king at one moment, in the way Joshua's long day was, Joshua 10:12 to 14. It does not promise that every sickness will reverse. What continues to apply is the character of God shown here: a God who hears, sees and acts, and who gives life so that He may be praised.

debates.question: If Isaiah says Hezekiah 'will not recover' and then God adds fifteen years, did God change His mind?

views.label: The word was a conditional warning
views.case: Many prophecies announce what will happen unless something changes. Jeremiah 18:7 and 8 states the principle, and Jonah 3:10 shows it at work with Nineveh. Hezekiah's prayer is the change that the warning was meant to produce, so the sentence and the reprieve fit together.

views.label: God truly responds in time to what His people do
views.case: The verbs of verse 5 are 'I have heard,' 'I have seen.' The text presents prayer as making a real difference, as in Exodus 32:14 and Amos 7:3, where the LORD 'relented.' On this view God's responsiveness is part of His character, not a figure of speech.

views.label: God ordained both the sentence and the prayer
views.case: Passages like Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say God does not change His mind as men do. Much of the Reformed tradition reads the sentence as a means by which God drew Hezekiah to pray, and the prayer as a means by which God had always intended to heal. The language of relenting is then God's way of speaking in human terms.

debates.bearing: All three views honour verses 5 and 6: the LORD heard, saw and healed. The chapter is not teaching that God's will is fragile, and it is not teaching that prayer is pointless. It teaches that God's stated word and His mercy are not at war, and that honest prayer is part of how He governs. Readers should be slow to turn this into a technique.

debates.question: Why does the Hezekiah section run in the order 36 and 37, then 38 and 39, if the illness came first?

views.label: Isaiah arranged by theme
views.case: The arithmetic of Isaiah 36:1, 2 Kings 18:2 and the fifteen added years puts the illness in the same year as the Assyrian invasion. Merodach-baladan's embassy, chapter 39, probably belongs to a similar time, and Assyrian records tell of Sennacherib defeating him early in his reign. Isaiah places the public deliverance first and Babylon last so that the section ends on the word that leads into chapter 40.

views.label: The events are close enough that order matters little
views.case: The promise of verse 6 treats Assyria as still present, so these are overlapping crises. The book has set them side by side and invites us to read them together, not to build a timeline.

debates.bearing: Either way, the lesson is the same. The book wants the reader to leave the Hezekiah story with two truths in mind: the LORD delivers, and the king who was delivered still carried the seed of the nation's later exile. The ordering serves that purpose.

debates.question: Is Hezekiah's despair about Sheol bad theology or honest lament?

views.label: An honest lament inside partial revelation
views.case: The psalms of Psalm 6, 30, 88 and 115 speak as Hezekiah does. They are not denying a future but grieving the loss of worship in the present, in the way Psalm 49:15 and Psalm 73:24 later reach for something more. The poem is faithful speech at the edge of what had been revealed.

views.label: A mistaken belief that Scripture corrects
views.case: The statement that the dead cannot hope in God's faithfulness is contradicted by passages like Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Hezekiah, under the strain of fear, speaks as if death were the end, and the New Testament shows how much more there was to know.

debates.bearing: Whichever way one leans, the chapter shows that Scripture records human prayer exactly as it was prayed, and that later revelation fills in what earlier believers could not yet see. It is also a comfort to know that God hears a lament that is not doctrinally complete.

study.originalLanguages:
The words in this chapter are worth slowing down for, because several of them carry far more than the English shows.

In verse 1 'put your house in order' is the verb tsavah, 'command' or 'give orders,' so the phrase is literally 'give instructions to your house.' It is the deathbed idiom for settling one's affairs, and the same idiom describes Ahithophel's last act before his suicide, 2 Samuel 17:23. The LORD's own word to the king is a request to prepare his household to be left.

In verse 3 Hezekiah 'wept bitterly,' literally 'wept a great weeping,' a verb joined to its own noun for emphasis. He also says he walked before God 'wholeheartedly.' The Hebrew shalem means whole, complete, undivided; Solomon urges Israel to have a heart so devoted, 1 Kings 8:61. Hezekiah is claiming singleness of heart, not sinlessness.

In verse 5 the LORD says, 'I will add,' from the verb yasaf, the verb Rachel used when she named Joseph, 'May the LORD add to me another son,' Genesis 30:24. Proverbs 10:27 says that the fear of the LORD 'prolongs' days, from the same root. Years are things that can be given.

Verse 8 says the LORD will make the shadow 'go back,' the verb shuv, the everyday word for turning and returning. It is also Scripture's word for repentance. The text does not play on this, but a shadow turned back and a king turned toward the wall belong to the same story of turning.

In verse 17 the Hebrew is blunt: 'for shalom I had bitterness, bitterness.' The BSB renders 'for my own welfare,' and the word is shalom, wholeness. Hezekiah concludes that his anguish served his shalom. The same word returns in the next chapter, where he comforts himself with 'peace and security in my lifetime,' Isaiah 39:8, and emet, the 'faithfulness' of verses 18 and 19, is the word the BSB renders 'security' there. The reader is meant to compare how he uses these words in song and in conversation.

He also says the LORD has 'cast' his sins behind His back, the verb shalak, which Micah 7:19 uses for casting sins into the depths of the sea.

Two footnotes are worth noticing. In verse 10 a translator's note offers 'In the quiet' or 'In the middle' for the Hebrew rendered 'in the prime of my life,' and in verse 13 'I composed myself' may instead be 'I cried out.' The poem's meaning does not change, but it shows how compressed the Hebrew is. In verse 6, one ancient witness adds 'for My sake and for the sake of My servant David,' which is the wording of 2 Kings 20:6.

typology.type: The prayer heard in the face of death, verses 2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: A king sentenced to die weeps, prays, and is heard. The New Testament says that in 'the days of Jesus' earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. The correspondence is real: the same tears, the same appeal to a faithful walk, the same Father. The escalation is that Christ's faithfulness is perfect, 'I always do what pleases Him,' John 8:29, and He prays 'not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42. The type falls short because Hezekiah is spared the sentence; Christ is heard by being raised through death.

typology.type: The third day and the house of the LORD, 2 Kings 20:5 and Isaiah 38:22
typology.fulfillment: In the parallel account Isaiah promises that 'on the third day from now you will go up to the house of the LORD,' 2 Kings 20:5, and the question that closes the Isaiah chapter is about that going up. Hosea 6:2 speaks of being raised 'on the third day,' and Paul says Christ 'was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4. The Old Testament does not say Hezekiah's recovery is a picture of the resurrection, so this is a pattern to hold gently. But the shape is worth noting: a man under a sentence of death is brought up on the third day to worship. The type falls short because Hezekiah recovered from sickness and later died; Christ rose from the dead.

typology.type: Brought up from the pit, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: Hezekiah says the LORD held him back from 'the pit of oblivion.' Jonah, from the fish, says 'You raised my life from the pit,' Jonah 2:6, and Jesus called that the sign He would give: 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth,' Matthew 12:40. In Christ the picture becomes actual: He enters the grave, and Peter says God did 'not abandon my soul to Hades,' Acts 2:27. The type falls short in that Hezekiah and Jonah came back to ordinary life and ordinary death, while Christ's resurrection is the first of the harvest, with His people to follow.

typology.type: Added years and the throne of David, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: The extra years kept the line of David alive: Manasseh was born after the recovery, and Hezekiah appears in Jesus' genealogy, Matthew 1:10. The LORD speaks as 'the God of your father David.' The fulfilment in Christ is that He is the Son to whom 'the Lord God will give the throne of His father David,' who 'will reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:32 and 33. The type falls short at once: the added years brought Manasseh, whose wickedness 2 Kings 21:9 and 23:26 name as a cause of Judah's fall. The true king does not owe his reign to borrowed years but to 'an indestructible life,' Hebrews 7:16.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by contrast more than by direct promise, and the contrast is instructive.

Hezekiah's sentence was an announcement that he would die; the LORD's response was to extend his years. Christ too was under a word of death, but He went through it. Hebrews 5:7 says He prayed with loud cries and tears 'to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard.' The same Father heard both men. For Hezekiah the answer was reprieve; for Christ the answer was resurrection. Gethsemane, with its 'if You are willing, take this cup from Me,' Luke 22:42, is the other half of this chapter. Hezekiah asked for the cup to pass and it did. Christ asked and drank it, because the world's sins were in it.

Hezekiah's words about the dead sound like the end of every hope. Christ takes the other side of those words. He says to the church, 'the gates of Hades will not prevail against it,' Matthew 16:18, and to John, 'I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:17 and 18. The silence of Sheol that Hezekiah dreaded is broken by the One who has been there. Where Hezekiah says that 'Sheol cannot thank You,' Paul answers, 'Death has been swallowed up in victory,' 1 Corinthians 15:54.

There is a gentler link in verse 17. Hezekiah says that the LORD has cast all his sins behind His back. That is the language of forgiveness, and the New Testament says how it was done: 'He forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt... nailing it to the cross,' Colossians 2:13 and 14, and 'Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more,' Hebrews 10:17. Hezekiah could say the sentence; Christ paid for it.

A further contrast helps. Lazarus was ill and his sisters sent word, and Jesus said, 'This sickness will not end in death,' John 11:4, and raised him. Yet Lazarus was given back time, not endless life, and so was Hezekiah. Both are pointers. The years Hezekiah got were a gift from the hand of God; the life that Christ gives is 'an indestructible life,' Hebrews 7:16.

It would be a mistake to read every detail of the chapter as a picture of Jesus. The fig poultice and the stairway are not coded. The links above rest on how the New Testament itself speaks of prayer in the face of death, of the pit, and of forgiveness.
study.god:
Three things about God stand together in this chapter, and the pull between them is the point.

He is the God whose word cannot be shrugged off. The sentence in verse 1 is 'This is what the LORD says,' and Hezekiah does not treat it as a medical opinion. Nor does he treat it as a fate. He takes it to God. The same voice that sentences is the voice that answers.

He is the God who listens and sees. 'I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears,' verse 5, is among the tenderest sentences in Isaiah. The God who 'sits enthroned above the circle of the earth' (a picture Isaiah 40:22 will soon state outright) attends to a sick man's weeping. Hezekiah's tears are named as something God saw. The text does not say Hezekiah deserved this, and in fact verse 17 credits the 'love' of the LORD for his rescue. The LORD acts out of faithful commitment, partly for His own name and for the promise to David, as the parallel in 2 Kings 20:6 says.

He is the God who governs the creation down to a shadow. That the sun's shadow could be turned back is not a decorative miracle. It declares that the one who numbers a man's days also holds the clock. This is Isaiah's larger claim in the chapters that follow: the God of Israel is Lord of history and of nature, with no rivals.

These three together shape how we think about God's sovereignty and prayer. His word is firm and He is not talked out of what is just. Yet prayer matters because it is the way His people are drawn into His purposes. The poem's final theme says what the life is for: 'The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD,' verse 20.

For worship, the chapter gives us a pattern of speaking to God out of fear. Hezekiah does not hide what he feels. He chirps like a swallow and moans like a dove. He says the LORD has broken his bones, and then he says, 'be my security.' A faith that can say both is honest, and God receives it. The same chapter also holds a warning: gifts of grace require grateful use. The next chapter shows what happens when that gratitude fades.

crossReferences.note: The parallel account, with details Isaiah leaves out: Isaiah had not left the middle courtyard when God spoke again, the promise of recovery on the third day, and the choice Hezekiah is given between the shadow going forward or back ten steps. It also records that the poultice was applied and he recovered. Reading both shows how Isaiah has moved the poultice to the end.

A short summary that adds a sober note: after his recovery 'his heart was proud,' and wrath came upon Judah until he and the people humbled themselves. This is the shadow behind Isaiah 39 and tells the reader that the story of gift and gratitude has a hard edge.

A song of someone healed from the brink of Sheol, with the same movement from cry to rescue. Verse 9, 'Will the dust praise You?' makes the same argument Hezekiah makes in verses 18 and 19. The two songs show how a rescued person speaks to God.

A lament that never gets its answer within the psalm, asking whether wonders, loving devotion and faithfulness can be known in the grave. It shows the darkest form of the question Hezekiah is asking, and why his recovery is such a relief.

Another prayer from the edge of death in which the LORD 'raised my life from the pit.' It uses the same word for the pit that Hezekiah uses in verse 17, and Jesus names Jonah as the sign pointing to His own burial and rising, Matthew 12:39 and 40.

A prophet's version of what Hezekiah says in verse 17: the LORD 'will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' Both use the picture of God disposing of sin, and Micah makes it a promise to a whole people, not one king.

Ahaz, Hezekiah's father, was told to ask for a sign as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven and refused. Hezekiah, in verse 22, asks. The father's pious refusal and the son's honest request show two ways of responding to a God who offers to confirm His word.

The New Testament picture of Christ praying 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death.' It is the closest verbal echo of Hezekiah's tears, and it shows how far the Son's prayer goes beyond the king's, since it ends in death and resurrection.

The closest parallel in the narratives, where the sun's course is altered, and the writer notes that 'the LORD listened to the voice of a man.' Together with Isaiah 38:8 it shows that the God of Israel answers prayer in the sky itself, and that neither event is presented as a model to expect again.

Paul's taunt, 'Where, O Death, is your victory?' takes up the very enemy Hezekiah feared in verses 10 to 18. What was a closed gate for a king in the eighth century before Christ becomes, in Christ, a defeated power.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world in which the first command was to live and enjoy God's presence. Genesis 3 brought death in, and from then on a frightened human voice runs through the Scriptures asking whether the grave is the end. Hezekiah's poem is one of the clearest of those voices. It is an Old Testament believer standing at the door of Sheol and saying exactly what he sees: silence, no praise, no more of the LORD in the land of the living.

The chapter answers that fear in a small way. A king is given fifteen years, a city is promised rescue, and a sign in the sky confirms it. But the story never lets the answer be complete. The extra years are used, then run out, and Hezekiah 'rested with his fathers,' 2 Kings 20:21. The gift postponed death; it did not end it.

That is why the chapter belongs where it does in Isaiah. The book moves from deliverance from Assyria to a personal deliverance to a prophecy of Babylon. A reader who hopes that God's help is simply the extension of the good life has to learn from the next chapter that the people will still go into exile, and from the rest of the book that the larger rescue is yet to come. The Servant of chapters 42 to 53 will go into death for others, and Isaiah 25:8 promises that God 'will swallow up death forever.'

The one story's real answer to Hezekiah's fear is Christ. He prays with tears and is heard in the sense that matters most: He passes through the gate and out of it, and now holds its keys, Revelation 1:18. The saints who share in His resurrection are the 'living' of whom Hezekiah spoke, and they do tell their children of His faithfulness.

The new creation fulfils the hope of verse 20 in full. The people of God do not merely get years to sing in the temple; they come to a city in which 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, and where God Himself is with them. The song that Hezekiah promised to sing 'all the days of our lives' goes on for all the days of eternity.

quiz.q: What word does Isaiah first bring to Hezekiah in verse 1?

options.text: That he is mortally ill and will not recover; he should put his house in order.
options.note: Verse 1 delivers exactly this sobering word from the LORD through Isaiah.

options.text: That his enemies will soon attack the city.
options.note: The word concerns Hezekiah's own health, not an external military threat.

options.text: That he will be given great wealth.
options.note: The word is a sentence of death, not a promise of wealth.

options.text: That his reign will be extended by fifty years immediately.
options.note: The initial word is a death sentence; the extension of years comes only after Hezekiah's prayer.

quiz.q: How does Hezekiah respond to this news in verses 2 to 3?

options.text: He turns to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly, reminding the LORD of his faithful life.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 describe exactly this tearful, honest prayer.

options.text: He accepts the news calmly with no prayer at all.
options.note: The opposite; he responds with fervent, tearful prayer, not passive acceptance.

options.text: He immediately summons foreign physicians instead of praying.
options.note: His first response recorded is prayer, not seeking foreign medical help.

options.text: He blames Isaiah for delivering the message.
options.note: He directs his response to the LORD in prayer, not blame toward the prophet.

quiz.q: What sign does the LORD give to confirm His promise in verses 7 to 8?

options.text: The sun's shadow on the stairway of Ahaz goes back ten steps.
options.note: Verse 8 describes this extraordinary sign exactly.

options.text: A sudden earthquake shakes Jerusalem.
options.note: The specific sign given is the reversal of the sun's shadow, not an earthquake.

options.text: A rainbow appears over the temple.
options.note: Not the sign described in this chapter; the sign concerns the sun's shadow.

options.text: A dream given to Hezekiah's son.
options.note: The sign is a visible, public reversal of the sun's shadow, not a private dream.

quiz.q: What reason does Hezekiah give in verse 19 for wanting to keep living?

options.text: Only the living can thank God, and fathers can tell their children about His faithfulness.
options.note: Verse 19 gives exactly this reason, connecting life to ongoing praise and testimony.

options.text: He wants to accumulate more wealth and possessions.
options.note: His stated reason concerns praise and testimony, not material gain.

options.text: He wants to avoid all future hardship entirely.
options.note: His reasoning centers on praising God and teaching the next generation, not merely avoiding hardship.

options.text: He wants to outlive his political rivals.
options.note: Not his stated reason; the text gives a reason rooted in worship and testimony, not political rivalry.

quiz.q: What does Hezekiah say the LORD has done with his sins in verse 17?

options.text: Cast all his sins behind His back.
options.note: Verse 17 states this directly, a vivid image of complete forgiveness.

options.text: Recorded them permanently for future judgment.
options.note: The opposite; the image is one of sins being removed from view, not preserved for judgment.

options.text: Forgiven only some of his sins.
options.note: The image of casting sins behind God's back conveys complete removal, not partial forgiveness.

options.text: Transferred them to his descendants.
options.note: Not the meaning of this verse, which describes God removing Hezekiah's own sins from view.

questions: Hezekiah wept bitterly and reminded God of his faithful life rather than accepting the news of death in silence. How honest are you with God when you receive news you cannot control?
Hezekiah's reason for wanting more years was to keep praising God and telling the next generation of His faithfulness. What would it look like for you to live your added days with that same purpose?
The LORD confirmed His word with a sign that reversed the ordinary course of the sun. Where do you need fresh confidence that God's promises to you are trustworthy, even without a visible sign?
Hezekiah rejoiced that his sins were cast behind God's back. Is there a sin you are still carrying that Christ has already fully removed at the cross?
Hezekiah's brush with death led to public thanksgiving in the house of the LORD. What has God rescued you from that you have not yet turned into open thanksgiving?

translationNotes.note: The stairway of Ahaz was likely a sundial-like structure whose steps marked the sun's shadow through the day; the sign reversed the shadow's ordinary movement.
This poem is presented as Hezekiah's own composition, a rare instance of a king's personal psalm preserved within a prophetic book.
These closing verses supply narrative details, the fig poultice and Hezekiah's request for a sign, that read almost as an appendix to the main account, paralleling similar detail in 2 Kings 20:7-8.
